explain.say: Hearing relies on about 15,000 delicate hair cells in each cochlea. Very loud sounds make the fluid around them surge so violently that they can be damaged.

explain.say: Damage depends on how loud the sound is and for how long. Each 10 decibel step is about ten times the sound energy, so a 110 decibel concert carries far more energy than busy traffic.

faq.q: How does loud noise damage hair cells?
faq.a: Very loud sound shakes the fluid in the cochlea so hard that the tiny bristles on hair cells bend too far, break or are worn out. Damaged cells stop sending signals for some sounds.
asks: How does loud music hurt your ears?
What happens to the ear in loud noise?

faq.q: Why do my ears ring after a loud noise?
faq.a: Ringing, called tinnitus, is a sign that hair cells have been stressed. The hearing system produces a sound signal even when there is no sound. Short ringing often fades, but it shows the ears were overloaded.
asks: Why do ears ring after a concert?

faq.q: Can hair cells in the ear grow back?
faq.a: In people and other mammals, hair cells in the cochlea do not grow back once they die. Birds and fish can regrow theirs, and scientists study them to understand why.
A decibel is a unit for measuring how loud a sound is. The scale goes up in multiplying steps: every extra 10 decibels means about ten times more sound energy.

faq.q: Why are high sounds lost first?
faq.a: High pitches are detected near the entrance of the cochlea, where every sound wave passes, so those hair cells take the most wear. That is why noise damage usually affects high pitches first.

facts: Each human cochlea contains roughly 15,000 hair cells.
An increase of 10 decibels means about ten times the sound intensity.
Mammals cannot regrow cochlear hair cells, but birds can.
